          <PC-AssayDescription_name>SAR analysis of Antagonists of XIAP-Bir3 domain of IAP-family anti-apoptotic proteins</PC-AssayDescription_name>
          <PC-AssayDescription_description>
            <PC-AssayDescription_description_E>Data Source: Sanford-Burnham Center for Chemical Genomics (SBCCG)</PC-AssayDescription_description_E>
            <PC-AssayDescription_description_E>Source Affiliation: Sanford-Burnham Medical Research Institute (SBMRI, San Diego, CA)</PC-AssayDescription_description_E>
            <PC-AssayDescription_description_E>Network: NIH Molecular Libraries Screening Centers Network (MLSCN)</PC-AssayDescription_description_E>
            <PC-AssayDescription_description_E>Grant Proposal Number: MH081277-01</PC-AssayDescription_description_E>
            <PC-AssayDescription_description_E>Assay Provider: John C. Reed, Sanford-Burnham Medical Research Institute, San Diego, CA</PC-AssayDescription_description_E>
            <PC-AssayDescription_description_E></PC-AssayDescription_description_E>
            <PC-AssayDescription_description_E>This dose response assay is developed and performed as a counter screen to compounds in the Chemical Antagonists of IAP-family anti-apoptotic proteins confirmation (AID 1449) and to study the structure-activity relationship on analogs of the confirmed hits. Compounds are either acquired from commercial sources or synthesized internally.  This assay was performed in the assay providers' laboratory.</PC-AssayDescription_description_E>
            <PC-AssayDescription_description_E></PC-AssayDescription_description_E>
            <PC-AssayDescription_description_E>Apoptosis plays an essential role in many aspects of normal development and physiology, becoming dysregulated in myriad diseases characterized by insufficient or excessive cell death. Caspases are intracellular proteases that are suppressed by Inhibitor of Apoptosis Proteins (IAPs), a family of evolutionarily conserved anti-apoptotic proteins. Proteins released from mitochondria (SMAC and HtrA2) can competitively displace IAPs from the Caspases, thus helping to drive apoptosis. It has been shown that only a few residues at the N-terminus of activated SMAC protein (4'mer) are sufficient to affect the release of IAPs from Caspases. Thus, it is plausible to identify chemical compounds that mimic the effect of SMAC in antagonizing IAPs by causing them to release Caspases. Non-peptidyl chemical inhibitors would have advantages over SMAC peptides, in terms of cell permeability, stability, and in vivo pharmacology. Thus, the goal of this project is to generate small-molecule chemical probe compounds that mimic the effects of SMAC peptides, inhibiting the function of IAPs.</PC-AssayDescription_description_E>
            <PC-AssayDescription_description_E></PC-AssayDescription_description_E>
            <PC-AssayDescription_description_E>Basis of the assay is disruption of fluorescence polarization resulting from binding of a XIAP-BIR3 (bacoloviral IAP repeat, "Bir3") domain protein derived from two of the three conserved caspase binding "BIR" domains of XIAP to a rhodamine tagged 7-mer N-terminal SMAC peptide.</PC-AssayDescription_description_E>
          </PC-AssayDescription_description>

Reed (Sanford-Burnham Medical Research Institute, San Diego, CA) and SMAC-rhodamine peptide (AVPIAQK-rhodamine) was provided by Richard Houghten (Torrey Pines Institute for Molecular Studies, San Diego, CA).</PC-AssayDescription_protocol_E>
